executive_summary: CAD/SGD closed at 0.91511 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in Singapore dollars per Canadian dollar, so a rising rate means a stronger Canadian dollar. It is up 1.64% over one month and 0.35% over three months, but down 1.47% over six months and 1.55% over one year. That leaves it at the 41st percentile of its 52-week closing range of 0.89689-0.94143. The pair rose 2.1% from its 12 October closing low, and almost all of that came from the Canadian side: markets repriced the Bank of Canada hike, WTI gained 14% in October and USD/CAD fell from its 1.43015 high, while USD/SGD hardly moved inside the MAS policy band. Looking at the two currencies against each other brings out three gaps that their US-dollar views do not show. On growth, Singapore grew 5.4% year on year in the third quarter and Canada grew 0.95%. On oil, Canada is a large crude exporter and Singapore is a net crude importer, so an oil move pushes the two currencies in opposite directions. On carry, holding the Canadian dollar against the Singapore dollar earns about 120bp a year in short rates. The tactical stance is Neutral, conviction 2 (score +0.004): the growth gap (-0.126) is almost exactly offset by three CAD-positive forces, namely a leveraged-fund CAD short close to its 2026 extreme that is vulnerable to a squeeze, an oil windfall that helps Canada and costs Singapore, and freshly hawkish Bank of Canada guidance. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2 (score -0.2732), because the Bank of Canada is unlikely to deliver the second hike the market prices, the MAS appreciating slope keeps compounding, and the threatened 1 January 2027 tariff increase hits Canada only. The caveat is that the strategic score is broad rather than deep: three of the four negative factors express the same theme, every confidence sits at 50-52, and a short position pays roughly 110 pips a year in carry. Our preferred expression is therefore to sell rallies into 0.9200-0.9230, where the 200-day average sits next to a nine-touch resistance zone, and target 0.8970 by end-April 2027. There is no listed option on this cross, so spot and forwards are the only instruments.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Real effective rates: real valuation favours the Canadian dollar. The BIS broad real effective rate for Canada is 95.59 (September 2026), the lowest reading since at least January 2024 and at the 3rd percentile of that window. Singapore's is 115.04, at the 88th percentile and second-highest in the G10+SGD set. The 19.45-point gap is the widest real-valuation spread in either currency's cross list after AUD/CAD. PPP: on World Bank GDP-based PPP, CAD/SGD fair value is 0.6779, so spot is about 35% above it. Both dossiers treat that gap as structural, because Singapore's measured price level is low relative to its income and the gap has not mean-reverted in decades; we do not use it as a target. What is priced: the cheap Canadian real rate prices a lasting tariff discount on Canadian exports and a Bank of Canada that stops early. The rich Singapore real rate prices an appreciating band through 2027 and a current account surplus near 17% of GDP. Neither prices the 1 January 2027 tariff decision in either direction. (52-week closing range is 0.89689-0.94143, with spot at the 41st percentile; the intraday range used above is 0.89537, hit on 9 October 2026, to 0.94669.)

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: A long CAD/SGD position earns about +120bp a year: the Bank of Canada's 2.50% overnight target less three-month compounded SORA of 1.297% (30 October). At spot that is about 110 pips a year, or about 9 pips a month. This is a policy-rate against money-market gap, not a forward funding differential, because no listed Singapore dollar future exists to measure one, and it ignores term premium and cross-currency basis. With no implied volatility the framework's carry-to-vol ratio cannot be computed (null); against realised volatility, carry over 60-day volatility is 0.36 and over 20-day volatility 0.38, respectable carry-to-risk readings for a cross. Carry regime: not working. The short-rate gap has been roughly 100-120bp through 2026, yet spot has fallen 1.55% over the year, so a carry-funded CAD/SGD long has lost about 0.4% after carry. The MAS band's appreciation, estimated at about 1.25% a year, has roughly cancelled the carry in trade-weighted terms, and the Canadian growth shortfall has done the rest. No traded CAD/SGD forward is observable. A synthetic cross forward (USD/SGD forward ÷ USD/CAD forward, using ING's 12 October USD/SGD points applied to the 30 October close, and USD/CAD forwards from the policy differential plus a near-zero basis) gives 0.91479 (1M), 0.91308 (3M) and 0.91041 (6M). Carry-equivalent rates at 120bp a year are 0.91419 (1M), 0.91236 (3M) and 0.90962 (6M). The two constructions agree to within 10 pips at three and six months; the one-month synthetic is distorted by stale USD/SGD points.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The short-rate gap favours the Canadian dollar. The Bank of Canada raised its overnight target 25bp to 2.50% on 28 October. Singapore has no policy rate, and three-month compounded SORA was 1.297% on 30 October, so a long CAD/SGD position earns about 120bp a year. That number is a policy-rate against money-market gap, not a forward funding differential, because no listed Singapore dollar future exists. In trade-weighted terms it is offset by the MAS policy band, which UOB estimates appreciates at about 1.25% a year. The Canadian hike was almost fully priced. Markets have since moved to a December hold and a January hike, and the CAD dossier puts only 55% on January, about 11bp less tightening than priced. On the Singapore side MAS left the band unchanged on 14 October. No MAS decision is on the published schedule for this period, and the dossier places the next statement in late January. SORA tends to drift with US rates, and a December Fed hike is about 77% priced. The Bank of Canada's next scheduled decision, on 9 December, is a bare statement without a Monetary Policy Report and falls just after the four-week window. Neither leg has a scheduled repricing inside four weeks, positive carry is roughly matched by the band's slope, and the residual mispricing on the Canadian path is small, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the relative path tilts against the Canadian dollar. The Canadian front end already discounts a second hike by January, with the 2-year 81bp above the policy rate. Meanwhile third-quarter growth is tracking about 1.3% annualised against the Bank's 2.0% projection, and CPI-trim and CPI-median are 1.8% and 1.9%. The CAD dossier expects 15-25bp of that tightening to be removed and gives a 40% chance that the Bank stops at 2.50%. The 9 December decision is the scheduled event that would start that repricing. The January Monetary Policy Report would extend it, but it is not on the published schedule for this period. On the Singapore side, three-month SORA has risen from a 1.06% second-quarter average to about 1.30% as US rates pass through. A Fed hike on 9 December would extend that drift, narrowing the CAD carry cushion from the SGD end. Meanwhile the MAS slope, estimated at about 1.25% a year, keeps lifting the band mid-point. Positive carry of about 120bp a year is the counterweight, and the reason confidence is only moderate: anyone short the pair pays it while waiting.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth and labour-market gap runs sharply in Singapore's favour. Singapore's third-quarter GDP rose 5.4% y/y and 1.1% q/q. September non-oil domestic exports rose 68.4% on a 107.6% jump in electronics, and unemployment is 2.0%. Canada's August GDP was flat and September is estimated at -0.1%. Employment fell 68,300 in September and unemployment is 6.5%. Inflation is closer: Canadian headline is 3.1% but core trim and median average 1.85%, while MAS core is 2.0%. So neither economy faces a core-inflation emergency. The sensitivity is asymmetric. The MAS band absorbs Singapore's domestic surprises, so Singapore data barely move the Singapore dollar. Canadian releases feed straight into Bank of Canada pricing. The pair's tactical response therefore comes mainly from the Canadian Labour Force Survey on 6 November, Canadian CPI on 16 November and third-quarter GDP on 30 November. October's Canadian releases have surprised to the downside on every major print except retail sales and trade, and the CAD dossier expects a third employment decline, so the tactical tilt is Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the gap narrows but stays wide. MAS expects Singapore's positive output gap to narrow through 2027 as AI-related exports lap a high base, with core inflation easing from mid-2027. Fourth-quarter growth near 4% would still leave 2026 around 5.5%. Canada faces a softer profile. The Reuters poll has fourth-quarter growth at 0.8-1.3% annualised, housing is contracting, and tariffs on C$20bn of exports are feeding through. Canada's hawkish risk is business inflation expectations of 3.7% one year out, which could lift core toward 2.3% if oil stays above USD 100. Singapore's equivalent risk is energy pass-through to transport and utilities. The cyclical phases differ: Singapore is decelerating from above potential, while Canada is near stagnation below its central bank's projection. That keeps the growth differential in Singapore's favour even after base effects, though with lower confidence than tactically because oil could rescue Canadian headline inflation and Bank of Canada hawkishness.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/SGD is a low-to-moderate risk-sensitivity cross. The Canadian dollar is mildly risk-positive, with a beta held down by its US linkage. The Singapore dollar is defensive: its band limits downside, and it tends to hold up against high-beta currencies in risk-off. In a broad risk-off the CAD dossier expects USD/CAD to rise 1-2%, while the SGD dossier expects USD/SGD to rise about 0.5%. A risk-off episode is therefore mildly negative for the pair. Current signals are mixed. The VIX was 17.2 at the 29 October close and touched 20 intraday on 30 October. US investment-grade and high-yield spreads are at the 95th-96th percentile of their one-year ranges, while equities sit near records. Oil is rising on supply disruption rather than risk appetite, so it is not a clean risk signal. A semiconductor correction is a Singapore-specific risk, because electronics drove September's export surge. That partly offsets the defensive profile of the Singapore dollar. With credit leaning cautious but equities firm, and with offsetting risks specific to each currency, the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk regime has fat tails on both sides. The Middle East war is in its ninth month, with Qatari mediation running alongside a US threat to strike after the midterms. A credit-led risk-off would lift the US dollar and hurt the Canadian dollar more than the band-managed Singapore dollar, which is negative for the pair. A dovish Fed repricing after the midterms would weaken the US dollar broadly, but the CAD dossier notes that the Canadian dollar gains less than higher-beta peers in that regime. The Singapore dollar gains through the band and Asian capital flows, which is mildly negative for the pair as well. Against that, the Singapore growth story rests on the AI investment cycle, which MAS itself lists as a downside risk. A sharp equity correction concentrated in technology would hit Singapore's export engine more directly than Canada's. These forces are two-sided and of similar size, so the factor stays Neutral with lower confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The terms-of-trade differential currently favours the Canadian dollar. NYMEX WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00 and Brent front-month reached USD 117.64. That is a windfall for Canada as an exporter and a cost for Singapore, a net crude importer, even after allowing for Singapore's refining and re-export margin. Canada keeps less of the rally than the headline suggests, because the Western Canada Select discount widened to USD 27 under WTI. Its external accounts nonetheless show the gain: a C$8.84bn second-quarter current account surplus, the first since 2022, and an August merchandise surplus of C$4.2bn against C$1.5bn expected. Singapore's surplus is far larger, at 16.7% of GDP in 2025, but it is driven by the AI electronics cycle rather than by oil, and it is already reflected in a real effective rate at the 88th percentile. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Inflation & Growth (0.21) and Policy & Rates (0.24) dominate, and they contribute very differently. The next Bank of Canada decision, on 9 December, falls just outside the window. Inflation & Growth is the largest single contribution at -0.126. Singapore is growing 5.4% with 2.0% unemployment, while Canada's economy stalled in August and lost 68,300 jobs in September. Canadian releases also transmit to the cross through rate pricing, while the band absorbs Singapore's. Against that, three CAD-positive factors add up to +0.13: a near-extreme leveraged short in the Canadian dollar alongside SGD length near the strong side of its band, an oil windfall that helps Canada and costs Singapore, and fresh hawkish guidance from the Bank of Canada that limits how far January pricing can fall. The net score of +0.004 is a Neutral built from real offsets. The base and quote dossiers are both Neutral tactically, and the bilateral view confirms that rather than adding an edge. What is priced is a stabilising Canadian labour market and an unchanged MAS band. Our edge is a likely third Canadian employment decline on 6 November, but it is balanced by squeeze risk in the CAD short and by oil. The path of least resistance is sideways, with Canadian data on 6, 16 and 30 November setting the tone, and the US midterms on 3 November and Canada's budget on 5 November adding event risk. strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.19), Guidance (0.12) and Inflation & Growth (0.12) carry two-thirds of the score. Policy & Rates is the largest contribution at -0.1248. Canada's front end prices a second hike by January that weak growth and sub-2% core inflation are unlikely to support, while SORA is drifting up with US rates and the MAS slope keeps compounding. Guidance adds -0.06, because the Bank of Canada has a record of reluctant tightening while MAS's upside-risk language makes its next move more likely a tightening. Inflation & Growth adds -0.0624 on a growth gap that narrows but stays wide. Event Risk adds -0.026, driven by the Canadian-specific tariff deadline of 1 January 2027 and a war distribution in which the more likely ceasefire hurts Canadian terms of trade. External Balance, the second-largest weight, is Neutral. The oil windfall and a cheap Canadian real effective rate (95.59 against Singapore's 115.04) offset the tail risks to oil and tariffs, which is why the score does not go further. The two dossiers reinforce each other: CAD is Bearish strategically and SGD Bullish. What is priced is a 2.75% Canadian peak by January, a fixed MAS band and a forward discount on the Canadian dollar of about 1.2% a year. Our edge is removal of the Canadian tightening and a modest hawkish tilt from MAS. The path of least resistance is lower, against a headwind of about 120bp of carry. The 9 December Bank of Canada decision is the first scheduled test, followed by the tariff deadline and the January statements. Conviction is held at 2 despite the size of the score: the main negatives share one theme, every confidence is close to 50, and carry pays the other side. A Canadian employment rebound or a US-Canada tariff deal would undo most of the case. An analyst's caution on the call: the direction stands, but one point should be said plainly. The October rebound of 190 pips was driven by exactly the two forces the strategic case needs to fade: Bank of Canada hawkishness and USD 100 oil. If both persist into December, the strategic thesis is a slow loser that pays carry the whole time. That is why we enter only on strength, with a defined stop, rather than at spot.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the CAD dossier ranks the Canadian dollar 8th of 11 and the SGD dossier ranks the Singapore dollar 3rd. On rank difference alone, short CAD/SGD is one of the wider strategic spreads for both currencies. It is carry-negative, though: shorting the pair pays about 120bp a year. Short CAD/NOK and long AUD/CAD or GBP/CAD earn carry while expressing the same Canadian weakness, so CAD/SGD ranks behind them among CAD shorts. Among SGD longs it ranks behind short EUR/SGD, where the carry cost is similar but the euro's terms-of-trade drag is larger, and roughly level with short AUD/SGD on fundamentals but cheaper in carry.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral (score +0.004, conviction 2): offsetting growth, positioning, oil and guidance forces with no central bank decision inside four weeks.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish (score -0.2732, conviction 2): a lower CAD/SGD over one to three months as the Canadian tightening path is repriced lower against an appreciating MAS band, against about 120bp a year of carry.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not measurable against a pair consensus: we found no published bank research forecast for CAD/SGD. Against the bank forecasts for the two US dollar legs, our view is below the implied direction.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not measurable for the pair itself. The leg forecasts (Reuters poll USD/CAD, 3 September; ING USD/SGD, 12 October) imply roughly 1% Canadian dollar appreciation against the Singapore dollar over twelve months, the opposite direction to our strategic stance.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The leg forecasts imply modest CAD strength against SGD because the Reuters FX poll expects a larger Canadian dollar gain against the US dollar, on an eventual trade deal, than ING expects for the Singapore dollar. Both forecasts predate key information. The Reuters poll was taken before Canada's flat August GDP, two months of employment declines totalling about 110,000 and the 50% tariff threat for January 2027. ING's forecast assumed a MAS slope increase that was not delivered. We weigh the Bank of Canada's limited room to tighten and the Canadian-specific tariff calendar more heavily than the poll does, and the MAS slope's compounding more than its October pause. Newer forecasts narrow the gap: an aggregated consensus of bank and trading-house USD/CAD forecasts dated 1 November 2026 shows Long Term 1.39 and Short Term 1.41; combined with ING's USD/SGD path these imply about 0.9078 for CAD/SGD in the short run (1.28 ÷ 1.41) and about 0.9065 longer term (1.26 ÷ 1.39), both 0.8-0.9% below spot, so leg consensus points the same way as our strategic stance but less than half as far as our 0.8970 base case. OCBC keeps a constructive medium-term view on SGD but sees limited scope for outperformance while the S$NEER sits in the upper band. Model-based retail forecasts sit near spot (one quantitative model: Outlook NEUTRAL, Short term Bullish, 1-year Soft, forecast -0.78% over 1 year; another frames potential price ranges between 0.9100 and 0.9200 over 1 to 6 months); neither is bank research and we give them little weight.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A lower CAD/SGD would beat the forward only if the decline exceeds about 0.6% over six months, the carry paid by a short. The payoff is larger expressed through legs or crosses that do not pay that carry.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If a US-Canada tariff deal arrives and oil stays above USD 100, the Canadian dollar could re-rate from a cheap real effective rate, and a short position would lose on both spot and carry.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge for mechanical reasons. Over four weeks, the CAD positioning squeeze risk, the oil windfall and fresh hawkish Bank of Canada guidance offset the growth gap, and no central bank decides in the window. Over one to three months, weight moves toward the relative policy path and guidance. There, the Bank of Canada's limited room to tighten into weak growth, MAS's appreciating slope and the Canadian-specific tariff deadline accumulate, while the short-dated positioning asymmetry fades.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 9 December 2026 Bank of Canada decision, a bare statement without a Monetary Policy Report, followed by the 1 January 2027 US tariff deadline on Canadian steel and cars. The next MAS statement is not on the published schedule for this period and is expected in late January.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: There is no tactical directional edge. The strategic bearish view should be built only after the early-November Canadian data cluster has tested the CAD short, and with the roughly 1.2% annual carry cost in mind. Building it through the legs or through higher-carry CAD crosses avoids paying that cost. In price terms: range-trade 0.9090-0.9210 through November; add strategic shorts on rallies into 0.9200-0.9230, or on a close below 0.9090 after 9 December; keep the 0.9270 stop as the line where the short-dated squeeze has won.

assumptions: Price data: daily closing prices for CAD/SGD cover 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30, with no weekend sessions in the series. Spot is 0.91511 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, so no trading sessions are missing between spot and valuation, and every level, distance and pip figure is anchored to that close.

Moving averages and zones: the averages, support and resistance zones and the 200-week figures are computed over the full stored history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars), not just the 130 sessions shown. Averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. The 14-day average true range is 0.0036, or 36 pips.

Support shortfall: only nine resistance zones and one support zone met the two-touch clustering threshold. The thin support side reflects a pair trading near the bottom of its long-run range, with few swing lows below spot. The support list was supplemented with round numbers (0.9000, 0.8900), daily-structure levels (0.9050) and the October closing base (0.8969-0.9000), each marked as supplementary. Zone distances are measured from spot to the zone centre. Resistance levels in the structured fields are zone centres; the support level 0.90974 is the lower edge of the computed support zone.
The Canadian policy rate in the supplied official series read 2.25% as of 26 October, because it predates the 28 October hike; 2.50% is used throughout.
The Canadian 10-year yield in the official series is a monthly reading (3.8825% as of 1 September) and is not quoted as a live level; the 30 October close of 3.799% is used instead.

No Singapore policy rate or 10-year series is supplied, because MAS targets the S$NEER band. Three-month compounded SORA (1.297%) serves as the Singapore short rate (quote_policy_rate), and the SGS 10-year yield is 2.24% (30 October).

No implied volatility exists for CAD/SGD, because no listed Singapore dollar option exists, and no forward funding differential exists, because no listed Singapore dollar future exists. Both are permanent features of the market. The 120bp carry is a policy-rate against money-market gap, not a funding rate. The forward table is an indicative synthetic built from the two leg forwards, cross-checked against a carry-equivalent rate, and is not a traded quote. Carry-to-volatility is shown against realised volatility only (0.36 on 60-day, 0.38 on 20-day).

Weight adjustments: Inflation & Growth up by 0.03 tactically and 0.02 strategically (widest bilateral differential, transmitted asymmetrically through Bank of Canada pricing); External Balance up by 0.02 tactically and 0.03 strategically (oil drives the two legs in opposite directions); USD Liquidity down by the full 0.05 on both horizons (non-USD cross). All weights sum to 1.00 on both horizons.

Bilateral trade: IMF DOTS 2024 goods flows show Canadian exports to Singapore of USD 1.6bn and imports of USD 1.1bn, a USD 0.5bn Canadian surplus. Singapore's mirror data record USD 2.8bn of imports from Canada and USD 1.1bn of exports to Canada, a normal mirror-data gap. Either way the flows are too small to drive the cross.

Consensus: no bank research forecast exists for CAD/SGD. Implied cross forecasts are derived by dividing the leg forecasts and are labelled as such. Model-based retail forecasts are cited for context only.

Scheduling and probabilities: the only scheduled policy decision confirmed for 1 November 2026 to 1 March 2027 is the Bank of Canada on 9 December 2026, with no Monetary Policy Report. The late-January MAS statement and January Bank of Canada decision are expected dates, not confirmed; the catalyst dates 2027-01-25 and 2027-01-27 and the NODX date 2026-11-17 are approximations of 'week 4 of January' and 'week 3 of November'. Scenario and event probabilities come from the two currency analyses, adapted to the cross.

Use of price data: no factor stance rests on this pair's own recent trading. Realised volatility and chart structure appear only in market structure (Factor 9), in the trade plans, and in the entries, targets, stops and invalidator levels.

Dossier dates: the report does not state the dossier dates separately, so the valuation date of 2026-11-01 is used for metadata. The 52-week range fields use the intraday range (0.89537-0.94669, 38th percentile); the closing range is 0.89689-0.94143 (41st percentile). The base_cftc_percentile of 72 is the combined CAD net positioning percentile within the 2026 window; no SGD futures percentile exists.
